prompt:
Local fixture (course titles are omitted):

```
Student        Enrolled   Course
sid name year  sid cid    cid dept
 1  Ada   2     1  DB     DB  CS
 2  Ben   1     1  OS     OS  CS
 3  Cat   2     1  LA     LA  MA
 4  Dev   3     2  DB
                3  DB
                3  OS
```

Student has four rows, Enrolled six and Course three. Dev has no enrolment. The attributes are student id `sid`, student `name`, study `year`, course code `cid`, and department `dept`.

Which expressions are equivalent to the one below? Select all that apply.

```formula
σ year=2 (Student ⋈ Enrolled)
where
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition after it is true
year: Student's year-of-study attribute
⋈: natural join: match relational tuples on shared attribute names (here sid)
Student, Enrolled: the lesson's relations
In words: the enrolments of year-2 students, with their student details. Options may also use ∪ (union) and π (projection: keep only listed attributes).
```

options.text:
```formula
σ year=2 (Student) ⋈ Enrolled
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
Student: the local relation of sid, student name and study year
year: study year
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
⋈: natural join on sid
In words: Filter Student to year two, then join its enrolments, retaining all joined attributes.
```
options.explanation: Correct. The predicate mentions only Student's attributes, so the selection can be pushed below the join.

options.text:
```formula
Enrolled ⋈ σ year=2 (Student)
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
Student: the local relation of sid, student name and study year
year: study year
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
⋈: natural join on sid
In words: Join enrolments to year-two students, retaining all joined attributes.
```
options.explanation: Correct. Natural join is commutative (attributes are named, not positional), so swapping operands changes nothing.

options.text:
```formula
σ year=2 (Student) ∪ Enrolled
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
Student: the local relation of sid, student name and study year
year: study year
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
∪: union: combine relational tuples from compatible headings
In words: Attempt to union year-two student relational tuples with enrolment relational tuples. Their headings differ, so the expression is not well typed.
```
options.explanation: Not even legal: ∪ needs union-compatible inputs, and Student and Enrolled have different headings.

options.text:
```formula
π sid (σ year=2 (Student)) ⋈ Enrolled
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
Student: the local relation of sid, student name and study year
sid: student identifier
year: study year
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
π: projection: retain the listed attributes, removing duplicates
⋈: natural join on sid
In words: Keep just the ids of year-two students before the join. The output lacks student names and years.
```
options.explanation: This drops name and year before the join, so the result has only (sid, cid). Same students, different relation.

workedExample:
```formula
σ p (R ⋈ S) ≡ σ p (R) ⋈ S
R ⋈ S ≡ S ⋈ R
where
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true
p: a condition that mentions only R's attributes (here year=2, on Student)
R, S: relations (here Student and Enrolled)
⋈: natural join
≡: is equivalent to: same result for any contents
In words: a filter on one input can be applied before the join, and the inputs of a join can be swapped.
```

1. Push-down rule (line 1): `year` is in Student only, so option A is valid.
2. Commutativity (line 2): option B is option A with the operands swapped.
3. Option C fails union-compatibility: ∪ (union) needs both inputs to have the same attributes.
4. Option D is a different heading: an equivalence must give exactly the same relation, attributes included. (Projecting early with π is valid only if you keep every attribute that is needed later, and here name and year are in the output.)

prompt:
A query computes the expression below, joining on customer id. Which rewrite is valid and most useful to an optimiser?

```formula
σ c.country='UK'
  ∧ o.total > c.credit_limit
  (Customer ⋈ Order)
where
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true
c.country, c.credit_limit: attributes of Customer: its country and its credit limit
o.total: an attribute of Order: the order's total
∧: and: both conditions must hold
>: is greater than
⋈: join on customer id
Customer, Order: the two relations
In words: UK customers' orders whose total exceeds the customer's credit limit.
```

options.text:
```formula
σ o.total > c.credit_limit (σ
c.country='UK' (Customer) ⋈ Order)
where
Customer: the customer input, including country and credit limit
Order: the order input, including total and customer id
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
⋈: join on customer id
>: greater than
c.country: customer country text
c.credit_limit: customer monetary credit limit
o.total: order total, in the same currency as the limit
In words: Filter Customer to the UK, join orders by customer id, then compare each order total with that customer’s credit limit.
```
options.explanation: Correct. Split the conjunction (cascade), push `country = 'UK'` down to Customer because it uses only Customer's attributes, and leave the comparison that spans both relations above the join.

options.text:
```formula
σ c.country='UK' (Customer) ⋈ σ
o.total > c.credit_limit (Order)
where
Customer: the customer input, including country and credit limit
Order: the order input, including total and customer id
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
⋈: join on customer id
>: greater than
c.country: customer country text
c.credit_limit: customer monetary credit limit
o.total: order total, in the same currency as the limit
In words: Attempt to test an order against a customer credit limit before joining. Order has no such attribute, so this is not well typed.
```
options.explanation: The second predicate mentions `c.credit_limit`, which Order does not have, so it cannot be evaluated below the join.

options.text:
```formula
σ c.country='UK' ∧ o.total >
c.credit_limit (Customer) ⋈ Order
where
Customer: the customer input, including country and credit limit
Order: the order input, including total and customer id
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
⋈: join on customer id
∧: and: both conditions must hold
>: greater than
c.country: customer country text
c.credit_limit: customer monetary credit limit
o.total: order total, in the same currency as the limit
In words: Attempt to test the full two-input condition on Customer alone. Customer has no order total, so this is not well typed.
```
options.explanation: Customer has no `total` attribute; only predicates over one relation's attributes can be pushed to it.

options.text: No rewrite is valid, because the predicate mentions both relations
options.explanation: The conjunction can be split (a selection on "p and q" equals a selection on p followed by one on q), and the part that mentions only Customer can then be pushed.

workedExample:
```formula
σ p∧q (X) ≡ σ q (σ p (X))
σ p (C ⋈ O) ≡ σ p (C) ⋈ O
σ q (σ p (Customer) ⋈ Order)
where
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true
p: country='UK', which uses only Customer's attributes
q: total > credit_limit, which uses attributes of both relations
∧: and
X: any relation
C, O: Customer and Order
Customer, Order: the two relations
⋈: join on customer id
≡: is equivalent to: same result for any contents
In words: split the "and" (cascade), push the UK filter below the join, and keep the comparison that spans both relations above it. The last line is the rewritten query.
```

q must stay above the join (or become part of the join condition, which is the same thing as a theta join). If 10% of customers are in the UK, the join's Customer input shrinks tenfold.
